entry.evidence: In view of recently reported discrepancies in mineral solubility results obtained with the classical diamond trap method

sequences.source_document: Publisher XML full text (jats_text), with PDF for figure pages

steps.action: Collected the three published accuracy tests of the classical diamond trap (Aerts et al. 2010, Tiraboschi et al. 2018, Rustioni et al. 2021), which report deviations from reference solubilities between 3% and more than a factor of two.
steps.quote: Rustioni et al. (16) found deviations from reference values ranging from 3% to more than a factor of two, even among identical experiments

steps.action: Drew on published work for candidate causes of classical diamond trap errors: minerals precipitating in the trap during the run (glass supersaturation, temperature gradients, HFSE oxides) and element fractionation during ablation of diamond+albite+H2O.
steps.quote: Minerals that precipitate within the diamond trap during this process will be misinterpreted as dissolved fluid components.

steps.action: Posed the aim of finding an alternative fluid-trapping approach that gives more reproducible high P–T fluid compositions than the classical diamond trap.
steps.quote: it is important to test alternative approaches that may lead to more reproducible results

steps.action: Built the single-crystal diamond trap: 9–16 laser-drilled holes (80 µm) in a synthetic diamond plate covered by a second plate, shrunk into a cut-open inner Pt capsule placed inside a larger Pt capsule with H2O and crushed minerals.
steps.quote: trapping the high P–T fluid in pre-drilled holes in single diamond crystals

steps.action: After direct epoxy filling of dried holes failed (spiky signals, Rb and Cs dissolving into the epoxy), developed melting of the precipitates with MnO-doped Li2B4O7 glass at 1000 °C under Au foil, followed by epoxy filling.
steps.quote: Attempts to directly fill the holes with epoxy and subsequently analyze them by LA–ICP–MS were not successful

steps.action: Designed test samples with known amounts of solids in the holes: fine Al2O3, TiO2, BaCO3 and CaF2 in epoxy (for calibration), and garnet, epidote and tourmaline pigments placed via Crystalbond 509 (to test the full melting procedure).
steps.quote: we prepared test samples with known amounts of chemicals or minerals that were placed into the drilled holes in the diamonds

steps.action: Checked blanks: analysed the MnO-doped Li2B4O7 and the epoxy by LA–ICP–MS (Tables S1, S2), and computed that the 0.37 wt.% SiO2 contamination adds at most 1.85% to the SiO2 result.
steps.quote: The purity of the MnO-doped Li2B4O7 and the epoxy was checked by LA–ICP–MS analyses.

steps.action: Reported that the first version, with Rb and Cs as internal standards in the fluid, gave poor reproducibility and too high or too low values in high P–T model-system runs, and that opening capsules frozen amplified the problem.
steps.quote: were plagued by poor reproducibility and in average either too high or too low values

steps.action: Replaced the fluid internal standard with the carbon signal of the epoxy filling (after trace-element-doped epoxy also failed through inhomogeneity), a standardless quantification relative to the epoxy weight.
steps.quote: which opens up the possibility to use the epoxy filling instead of a fluid component as the internal standard

steps.action: Calibrated the quantification by fixing a fictive epoxy carbon content of 100 wt.% and fitting the calcite carbon content (15 wt.%) with Excel goal seek to the doped-epoxy test samples.
steps.quote: changed via the "goal seek" analysis tool in Excel the carbon content of the calcite until the best average result was obtained

steps.action: Checked the stability of the fictive carbon calibration by analysing test samples on 15 measuring days over 5 months with a constant value; results were consistent.
steps.quote: test samples analyzed on 15 different measuring days spread over a 5 months period using a constant fictive carbon value for the calcite

steps.action: Added corrections: normalization of all concentrations to a solvent density of 1.00 g/cm3, then correction to the actual solvent density, and an iterative correction for hole volume occupied by precipitates plus Li2B4O7 (stable after three iterations).
steps.quote: we decided to normalize all concentrations to a solvent density of 1.00 g/cm3

steps.action: Showed representative hole-by-hole LA–ICP–MS signals, with the epoxy carbon signal about six times the diamond carbon signal, so the integrated carbon is dominated by epoxy.
steps.quote: The net carbon signal obtained from the ablation of epoxy is about 6 times higher than the net signal obtained during the ablation of diamond

steps.action: Compared melted pigment tests (garnet, epidote, tourmaline) with weighed-in values (5–16% agreement) and with LA–ICP–MS analyses of pressed pellets of the same powders (within 1 wt.%, except tourmaline Al2O3 and one epidote K2O).
steps.quote: the obtained results agree with these reference values within 5–16%

steps.action: Tested element losses and gains during melting with GSE-1G reference glass plus Li2B4O7 in the holes: major elements unmodified, Na2O +50% and K2O +130%, several trace elements lost.
steps.quote: most of the major and minor element concentrations remained unmodified, except for Na2O and K2O

steps.action: Melted albite powder in the holes: SiO2, Na2O and Al2O3 within 2% of the starting material, but K2O gained, set against the factor-of-two SiO2/Al2O3 error of the classical trap (Rustioni et al. 2021).
steps.quote: SiO2, Na2O and Al2O3 concentrations that agree within 2% with those of the starting material, but about 3.8 wt. % K2O were gained

steps.action: Ran real piston-cylinder solubility experiments at 1.0 GPa, 800 and 900 °C in quartz–H2O and forsterite–enstatite–H2O (reference data exist) with SCDT, plus classical diamond trap runs at identical conditions.
steps.quote: the experiments were expanded to real solubility measurements at high pressure and temperature in the well-studied H2O–SiO2 and H2O–enstatite–olivine systems

steps.action: Compared measured with reference solubilities: SCDT +8%/+11% (quartz) and +21%/−11% (Fo+En), classical trap −20%/−56% and −31%/+7%; overall average deviation 13% for SCDT against 28% for the classical trap.
steps.quote: the new SCDT method produced results that deviate maximal 21% from the reference values (average deviation 13%)

steps.action: Proposed explanations for the classical trap discrepancies: thermal gradients, run duration, preferential H2O loss raising Cs, and Cs-rich residual solution expelled on opening the frozen trap.
steps.quote: One potential explanation would be preferential loss of H2O during the experiment

steps.action: Argued against thermal gradients (nearly 100 °C would be needed) and against run duration (SCDT runs were shorter yet accurate; classical runs of similar duration elsewhere were correct) as causes; the remaining explanations were left open.
steps.quote: Run duration should not have been the problem either

steps.action: Ran an SCDT experiment on crushed eclogite (2.8 GPa, 700 °C) at a high fluid/solid ratio and recovered large pyroxene, garnet and mica crystals after 15 h.
steps.quote: recovered large crystals of pyroxene, garnet and mica after a run duration of only 15 h

steps.action: Ranked uncertainty sources and computed the solubility error from a ±50 °C thermocouple–sample offset (from the authors' group's capsule temperature mapping, Audétat et al. 2020): 28% (Fo+En) and 14–43% (quartz).
steps.quote: A temperature offset of ± 50 °C at our experimental conditions results in a SiO2 solubility difference

steps.action: Used the separate holes as replicates within each experiment, identifying and excluding strongly anomalous holes in five of fifteen SCDT experiments.
steps.quote: in five of our fifteen SCDT experiments some holes were strongly anomalous and thus were not considered in the calculation of the average

steps.action: Varied the assumed precipitate and solute density by 30% (2–3% change in result) and checked the carbon sensitivity for drift over 15 days (no systematic shift).
steps.quote: changing the value by 30% causes the calculated concentration of dissolved matter to change by only 2–3%

steps.action: Stated the method's disadvantages and limits: time-consuming preparation and quantification, alkali gain or loss during melting, and the cost of the diamond plates.
steps.quote: Alkalies may be gained or lost during the melting step.

steps.action: Kept the claim that SCDT is a viable, more reproducible and more accurate alternative to the classical diamond trap, at least in this lab.
steps.quote: the SCDT method is a viable alternative to the classical diamond trap method and provides reliable mineral solubility data in high P–T fluids

tree.answer: Yes: published classical diamond trap solubilities deviate erratically from reference values.
No: fluid composition at P–T is inferred from quenched precipitates analysed by LA–ICP–MS.
Build and characterize a new fluid-trapping and quantification method.
SCDT against the classical diamond trap; candidate causes of classical trap errors.
Reference solubilities and weighed-in standards give expected values for both methods.
Set in the laboratory: piston cylinder at 1.0 GPa, 800–900 °C, and prepared test samples.
Mostly: survives reference glass, albite, density and day-to-day checks; alkalies are not reliable.
SCDT kept as more accurate (average 13% against 28% deviation).
Not documented; reviewers acknowledged but no review file.

end.claim: The single-crystal diamond trap with carbon-signal standardless quantification reproduces known and reference concentrations within 1–21% (average 13%), against 7–56% (average 28%) for classical diamond trap runs at identical conditions, but alkalies are mobile during the melting step.

decisive_move.sentence: Replacing the failed fluid internal standard (Rb, Cs) with the carbon signal of the epoxy filling made quantification of the melted hole contents possible; every reported result depends on this standardless procedure.

gates.evidence: The design (confined holes, evaporation, melting) was directed by stated hypotheses about precipitation and fractionation errors (§1 ¶5). The real experiments were chosen in systems with literature reference values that SCDT could have missed, as the earlier Rb/Cs version did (§2.4 ¶1; §3 ¶5). The reference values were fixed before the data, and the fictive carbon calibration was set on doped-epoxy samples and held constant (§2.4 ¶4). The exclusion of anomalous holes was decided after the data, without a stated threshold (§4 ¶3).

imports.item: LA–ICP–MS (GeolasPro 193 nm ArF excimer laser with Elan DRC-e quadrupole MS)
excimer laser drilling of holes in diamond
lithium tetraborate (Li2B4O7) flux melting of residues to glass
epoxy resin (EPOFIX) and Crystalbond 509 as hole fillings and carriers
NIST SRM 610 and USGS GSE-1G reference glasses
saturation properties of water (Saul and Wagner 1987) for solvent density
Excel goal-seek optimization for the fictive carbon calibration
Peltier-cooled LA–ICP–MS sample chamber for frozen classical traps

novelty_claims.quote: [...] to quantify the composition of high P–T fluids was developed
we developed a new quantification procedure that works without any internal standard in the fluid
[...] a new method that aims at minimizing the potential problem of mineral precipitation within the diamond trap
Our newly developed SCDT method for studying fluid compositions in high-P and high-T experiments offers the following advantages

limits:
No review file, discussion or earlier version was supplied, so there is no review sequence. The acknowledgements thank Müntener, Luth and an anonymous reviewer (§A1/acknowledgements, PDF p. 12), but what they changed is unknown.

The headline accuracy rests on few runs: 4 SCDT and 4 classical high P–T solubility runs. The "15 experiments" include 11 ambient-condition test samples (Table 1).

Inference: the doped-epoxy samples used to fit the fictive carbon value (§2.4 ¶4) also appear among the accuracy results (Table 1, deviations −19% to +9%), so that part of the accuracy figure is partly circular.

The abstract says 700–900 °C, but the solubility runs are at 800 and 900 °C; 700 °C is only the eclogite run (Table 1).

The earlier failed Rb/Cs high P–T experiments are described but not tabulated (§2.4 ¶1). About one in six capsules leaked (§2.1 ¶1). Criteria for excluding anomalous holes are not given beyond "strongly anomalous" (§4 ¶3).

Sub-claims at other statuses:
- Reduced ablation fractionation in SCDT: best_explanation, from one albite test set against one cited classical trap test (§3 ¶4; §4 ¶4).
- Causes of classical trap discrepancies: no_conclusion; two causes argued against, two left open (§3 ¶5).
- Suitability for partition-coefficient work through large crystal growth: capability_characterized only qualitatively, from one eclogite run (§3 ¶6).
- Alkalies and some trace elements (Cs, Cu, Ag, Cd) are not reliably recovered (§3 ¶3).

Composition is none_fits: the walk is problem-driven method validation. A question comes first, then a capability is built and revised after failures, then it is tested against weighed-in standards, reference glasses and literature reference solubilities, with the rival classical method run as a baseline. capability_first does not fit because the question and the rival precede the capability.

disagreements.target: Aerts et al. (2010) and Tiraboschi et al. (2018), single-experiment accuracies of 3% and 5% for the classical diamond trap
disagreements.support: The authors' own classical diamond trap runs at identical conditions deviated by 7–56% from reference values, agreeing instead with the scatter of Rustioni et al. (2021).
disagreements.quote: The same experiments performed using the classical diamond trap method show 20% deviation at 800 °C and 56% deviation at 900 °C.

disagreements.target: Classical diamond trap method as the most versatile and established technique (Ryabchikov et al. 1989; Kessel et al. 2004)
disagreements.support: Side-by-side runs against reference solubilities give an average deviation of 13% for SCDT and 28% for the classical trap, stated as valid in their lab.
disagreements.quote: the new SCDT method provides more reliable mineral solubility data at high P–T conditions than corresponding data obtained with the classical diamond trap technique

disagreements.target: Basic assumption of diamond trap experiments that everything in the trap was dissolved in the fluid at quench
disagreements.support: Cited in-situ observations of glass dissolution (Keppler 2017) and HFSE oxide precipitation in temperature gradients, plus HFSE signal peaks at 100–200 µm scale.
disagreements.quote: However, this assumption may not always be valid.

disagreements.target: Freezing technique with Cs internal standard (Kessel et al. 2004; Aerts et al. 2010)
disagreements.support: Proposed, without direct test, that Cs-rich residual solution or H2O loss biases Cs-normalized results; in their own holes freezing amplified internal-standard problems.
disagreements.quote: Another potential explanation is that during the opening of the frozen diamond trap some Cs-rich, residual solution was expelled onto the diamond trap surface.

alternatives_considered.chosen: Carbon signal of the epoxy filling as standardless internal reference
alternatives_considered.alternatives: Rb and Cs doped into the fluid as internal standard; trace-element-doped epoxy as internal standard
alternatives_considered.reason: Rb/Cs dissolved into epoxy and gave poor reproducibility; doped epoxy could not be made homogeneous at the micrometre scale

alternatives_considered.chosen: Evaporation of the fluid and melting of the residue with MnO-doped Li2B4O7 before epoxy filling
alternatives_considered.alternatives: Filling dried holes directly with epoxy
alternatives_considered.reason: Loose precipitates ablate fast and give very spiky signals
Pure Li2B4O7 glass is difficult to ablate with the laser

alternatives_considered.chosen: Opening SCDT capsules at room temperature
alternatives_considered.alternatives: Opening capsules frozen and letting the ice dry slowly
alternatives_considered.reason: Freezing did not solve and apparently amplified the internal-standard problem

alternatives_considered.chosen: Fictive epoxy carbon of 100 wt.% with fitted calcite carbon content
alternatives_considered.alternatives: True calcite carbon content with a fitted fictive epoxy carbon content
alternatives_considered.reason: The former approach is more practical for the calculations

alternatives_considered.chosen: Precipitates assumed to be SiO2 glass with SiO2-glass density
alternatives_considered.alternatives: Other precipitate or dissolved-matter densities (varied by 30%)
alternatives_considered.reason: Dissolved matter dominated by SiO2; chosen for simplicity

alternatives_considered.chosen: Short run durations (2–5 h for SCDT)
alternatives_considered.alternatives: Longer runs (5–10 h in their classical runs, 16–48 h in cited studies)
alternatives_considered.reason: Long runs promote dissolution–reprecipitation in thermal gradients and positive deviations

alternatives_considered.chosen: Exclusion of strongly anomalous holes from the average
alternatives_considered.reason: Anomalous holes attributed to mineral growth or preparation losses
